Both new findings fixed on `fix/cluster1-remainder`, not pushed. HEAD is now d544009.

**D** (ccc15b6) — `internal/session/store_windows.go`'s `isProcessAlive` now calls `windows.OpenProcess` directly instead of `os.FindProcess`, so it can distinguish `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` (process exists, this caller can't open it — e.g. owned by another user) from `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` (OpenProcess's confirmed-not-found signal for a genuinely dead PID). Every error except the confirmed-not-found one is now treated as alive — fail-closed on the asymmetry you described (false-dead purges a live pointer with no recovery; false-alive just leaves a stale pointer that self-heals at the next SessionStart). Not independently testable in this repo's CI (Linux-only; this file only compiles under GOOS=windows) — said so plainly in the commit rather than fabricating a test.

**E** (d544009) — verified the actual mechanism rather than reasoning about it: read Go's `syscall_windows.go` directly. `O_APPEND` on Windows clears `GENERIC_WRITE` and sets only `FILE_APPEND_DATA` — so the `O_APPEND|O_WRONLY` handle in `appendTraceSummary` carried neither `GENERIC_READ` nor `GENERIC_WRITE`, exactly what `LockFileEx` requires. Both new tests instead exercise the real locking path on every platform this CI does run — a genuine regression guard for the refactor, not a substitute for Windows coverage. tool_input.content:
`internal/identity` and `internal/claudemd` carry `!windows`-tagged flock implementations whose Windows counterparts stub-and-error rather than actually locking. PR #507 gave `internal/session` and `internal/mission` real `LockFileEx` implementations; these two are now the odd ones out.

## Why this is worth raising rather than leaving

A stub that returns an error is honest, and is genuinely better than a stub that silently no-ops — the caller at least knows. But it means those packages have no working concurrency control on Windows at all, while their siblings now do. That inconsistency is the problem: a reader encountering `internal/identity`'s stub reasonably concludes "this repo does not really lock on Windows", which is no longer true, and may copy the weaker pattern into new code.

PR #507 chose the stronger standard deliberately. `internal/session`'s lock guards the session pointer that DES-074's whole fix depends on, so a lock that does not lock was not acceptable there. The same reasoning applies to identity and claudemd writes, just with lower stakes.

## Scope

Both packages already have the `!windows` split; this is filling in the Windows side, not restructuring. Follow the pattern established in `internal/session/store_windows.go` and `internal/mission/flock_windows.go`:

- `LockFileEx`/`UnlockFileEx` via `x/sys/windows` (already a direct dependency).
- Carry the shared-vs-exclusive distinction if the caller has one — `internal/mission` needed a `lockShared`/`lockExclusive` mode parameter because flattening it would have silently serialised readers. Check whether identity/claudemd have the same distinction before assuming a single lock mode suffices.
- Note the semantic differences that matter: `LockFileEx` is mandatory rather than advisory, handle-scoped rather than fd-scoped, and has no atomic shared→exclusive upgrade.

Also check the handle's access rights. PR #507 found that `O_APPEND` on Windows clears `GENERIC_WRITE` and sets only `FILE_APPEND_DATA`, so an append-only handle carries neither access right `LockFileEx` requires — the fix was to lock a dedicated sibling `.lock` file, which is this repo's existing convention elsewhere. If identity or claudemd lock an append-only handle, they will hit the same wall.

## Testing limitation, stated up front

This cannot be verified in CI. The repo's CI is Linux-only and these files only compile under `GOOS=windows`, so `GOOS=windows go build ./...` exiting 0 proves compilation and nothing about lock behaviour. PR #507 hit the same limit and said so rather than implying coverage it did not have. Whoever picks this up should do the same, and should consider whether a portable test of the *calling* code's locking path (as #507 added for `appendTraceSummary`) is worth more than another build check.

## Related

- ethos PR #507 — where `internal/session` and `internal/mission` got real implementations, and where this divergence was noticed
- `ethos-cm2r`, `ethos-298s`, `ethos-qtp2` — the Windows build work that surfaced it

tool_input.content:
`GOOS=windows go vet ./...` fails on `_test.go` build-tag mismatches: portable (untagged) test files call helpers that live only in `!windows`-tagged test files.

Confirmed example: `internal/session/tombstone_purge_test.go` has no build tag but calls `testStore()`, which is defined in `store_test.go` under `//go:build !windows`.

## Pre-existing, and only now reachable

This is not a regression from PR #507. The mismatch has been there; it was simply unreachable, because `internal/session` did not compile under `GOOS=windows` at all — the build failed long before vet could reach the test files. #507 made the packages build on Windows, which surfaced it.

`make check` never runs `vet` or `test` under `GOOS=windows` — only `go build` does — so this does not fail any gate today and was correctly left out of #507's scope rather than scope-crept into a PR already under review.

## Why file it rather than ignore it

Windows is not a supported target, so this is P4. But it is worth recording for two reasons.

First, it is a trap for whoever picks up Windows support next: `GOOS=windows go build ./...` now exits 0, which reads as "Windows works", and the next person will reasonably run `go vet` or `go test` and hit a wall that has nothing to do with their change. Recording it means they find the explanation instead of re-deriving it.

Second, the fix is genuinely small — regate or rename a handful of test helpers so the portable test files can reach them — and is much cheaper than the work that surfaced it. It is a good first task for anyone extending Windows support.

## Scope

Audit `_test.go` files in packages that now compile under `GOOS=windows` (`internal/session`, `internal/mission`, `internal/process` at minimum) for the pattern: an untagged test file calling a helper defined only in a `!windows`-tagged one. Either give the helper a portable home or tag the caller to match.

Do not chase this beyond a clean `GOOS=windows go vet ./...`. Making the test *suite* pass on Windows is a separate and much larger question — the tests assume POSIX process semantics in places, and nobody runs them there.

## Related

- ethos PR #507 — made these packages compile on Windows, surfacing this
- `ethos-cm2r`, `ethos-298s`, `ethos-qtp2` — the Windows build chain
- `ethos-xa99` — the other Windows follow-up from the same PR

tool_input.message:
Pushed d544009, both follow-up beads filed (ethos-xa99 flock stubs, ethos-8r2i vet tag mismatches). Five new findings — one real, four doc-accuracy. All cheap. Same branch, don't push.

**F — REAL. `missions.jsonl.lock` evades gitignore.** `internal/mission/trace.go`.

Your fix creates `missions.jsonl.lock` beside the TRACKED `missions.jsonl`, and the existing ignore rule does not cover it. So the lock file becomes an untracked file in every repo that runs a mission, and the first `git add -A` commits it.

That is not cosmetic here. `missions.jsonl` is the tracked mission trace — the audit artifact — so its directory is one people deliberately commit. A committed lock file is both noise in the audit record and a live hazard: a stale `.lock` arriving via `git pull` on a machine that never created it. Check what the ignore rule actually matches and extend it. Verify with `git status --porcelain` after an append that the lock file does not appear as untracked.

Worth noting this is the same class as the release preflight failing on untracked mission artifacts earlier today — files the tooling creates that the ignore rules do not anticipate.

**G — `internal/mission/flock_unix.go`** comment calls the Windows implementation a "stub". No longer true — `flock_windows.go` is real `LockFileEx`. Fix it.

**H — `internal/session/store.go`**, `WithSessionLock` doc comment still says "exclusive flock" / "one flock per session". Now platform-specific. Reword to describe the behaviour rather than the POSIX mechanism.

**I — CHANGELOG entry for the session-end hint** says it prints when `ETHOS_SESSION` "is set". The code prints only when it matches the session just ended — that was finding A. The entry describes the PRE-FIX behaviour, which is the bug we fixed, documented as though it shipped.

**J — grammar**, `flock_unix.go`: "an flock" → "a lock", two occurrences (also line 26).

G, H and I are all one thing: this change made several comments false, and I is the worst of them because a CHANGELOG is what users read. Sweep the packages you touched for any other comment or doc still asserting flock/POSIX-only behaviour, rather than fixing only the three that were caught. That is the same fix-the-class point from earlier today, and a stale comment contradicting the code is exactly the defect we opened this cluster with (ethos-lldo, the commit-msg header).

`make check` per commit, detached gate with both counts, full `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...`. Report and I push.
